en: 1.a Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels. 2.b His feet are worshipped by the multitude of sages; he has destroyed all defects and possesses supreme glory.
Victorious is the Jina, skilled in the welfare of the entire world, who abides in pure awakening; he who is glorious, whose lotus feet are incessantly worshipped by gods and asuras alike,
the manifest treasury of merit, the supreme auspiciousness, the wish-fulfilling gem, and the omniscient one.

May the Blessed One, the son of Śuddhodana, the Victor and Lord of Sages, whose mass of faults has been entirely uprooted, who has reached the further shore, and whose splendor blazes forth, protect you!
Immediately following this, he states the introductory narrative (nidāna) for this edifying tale (avadāna). 5.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, though already knowing [the answer], spoke thus to the Blessed One for the sake of others:
"Blessed One, when does the *kaṭhina* arise?
The Blessed One said:

Starting from the first day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, during the thirty days, on whichever day and night the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṅgha arises, that [robe] must be caused to be brought with its fringes intact. Having had the border-fringe (*daśā*) and the dyeing performed according to the rule, and having had it prepared with blue thread, needles, and a razor according to the rule, the donors should cause it to be spread when the Saṅgha has assembled.
The monk acting as the *karmakāraka* should then greet the donors with a discourse on the preparation for giving.
Regarding that, starting with "one should dwell together," etc.:

a donor who wishes to provide the *kaṭhina* robe-material should approach the noble Saṃgha with humility during the month of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa and make a formal request through the mouth of the *kalpikāraka*. By him—
And it should be performed in this manner:
"Pay attention, noble Saṃgha! This person named so-and-so will spread the kaṭhina.
If the noble Saṃgha consents, let it be; if not, please withhold your consent."
At that time, if the intention of the donor is pure and the object to be given is perfectly pure, then he should accept it by remaining silent; otherwise, he should refuse it.

If the Noble Saṅgha then consents, the *kalpikāraka* (the officer in charge of allowable items) should dye a pair of well-measured and beautiful robes and show them to him. Then, taking those robes and dismissing the donor, he should measure them with his hand, thinking: "With these, I shall make the *kaṭhina* robe."
One should present it to him, saying, "It is for the donor.
For there are two kinds of *kaṭhina* robes: those that are made and those that are not made.

Among these, the "made" type—according to the divisions of the schools—is one consisting of three or five patches and so forth; it must be well-sewn, with a width of no less than three cubits and a length of no less than five cubits.
It is unmade, not sewn, and unaltered;
furthermore, each of these is of two kinds: finished and unfinished.
Among them, that upon which blue dots have been applied and which has been consecrated with the worship-mantra is "finished."

The other is not yet completed. Here, on the full moon day of Āśvina, the distributor of the robe-material for the donor, having prepared the *kaṭhina* robe according to the rules, takes it and, standing before the noble Saṃgha who has entered the three-month retreat, should speak as follows:
"Pay attention, noble ones! With this robe-cloth, a donor named Amuka shall spread the *kaṭhina* in this monastic residence.
May the noble Saṃgha grant its assent; may the donor rejoice.
Having thus requested a second and a third time, the noble Saṃgha, having accepted that request, [during the day...]
Having applied four drops at the edge with ink-liquid or a blue-colored dye— purified by the Four Truths and so forth—
or three, purified by the Three Jewels and so forth, or two, purified by the equipment for yoga and so forth— one should consecrate this according to the ritual procedure.

When the night has turned to dawn, in a place prepared and consecrated—one where parasols, banners, and flags are raised; where incense burners containing fragments and balls of incense are placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions; where bright staff-lamps are set out; and which is strewn with fragrant substances and divine, sweet-smelling flowers—one should worship the mantra-empowered [deity] upon a couch, a bed, or a broad seat with the five offerings.

Having spread out the kaṭhina robe, one should establish it. Thereafter, that faithful donor, having honored it with sublime offerings and having prostrated before it, [should offer] materials consisting of the elements such as gold,
silver, and copper, jewels such as emerald, ruby, diamond, lapis lazuli, sapphire, and so forth, as well as divine garments, ornaments, and the like.
And one should give that kaṭhina robe to the Triple Gem.

One should write down on a palm leaf or similar material the names of the external wealth—such as fields, houses, gardens, groves, and so forth; female and male slaves, elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, and the like; and the income from rents and other sources—and present that very document [to the recipient].

One should also give edible foods, drinks, things to be licked, things to be sucked, and so forth; vessels and the five types of utensils and implements; beds, seats, and the like; and medicinal drugs.
And having touched the kaṭhina with various implements and articles suitable for use, he should distribute it from its side for the enjoyment of the Saṃgha.
Thus [ends the section on] the kaṭhina.
7.b Then the venerable monk named Sumanas said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhagavān, for what reason is the robe and so forth called *kaṭhina*?
The Bhagavān said:
"Venerable one, that which is firm, pure, indestructible, and vast and imperishable is called *kaṭhina*."

For it is thus: because of the firmness of the donor's intention, the purity of the robe, the indivisibility of the Saṅgha, and the vastness and indestructibility of the fruit of the gift, everything indeed becomes *kaṭhina*.
[In] the city of Śrāvastī, the Charioteer who tames men...
Having dwelt thus, his mind liberated from all bonds,
with senses stilled and his heart at peace, the Jina invited his own disciples.

In the great city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the delightful park of Anāthapiṇḍada— which was perfumed with fragrant incense, adorned with heaps of sweet-smelling flowers, and possessed a pure precinct—

the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord Śākyamuni, the Great Compassionate One who has attained pure awakening and destroyed all afflictions, was dwelling together with a great multitude of assemblies, seated upon a vast and most precious throne.
Then the Blessed One, remaining in silence, directed his worldly mind toward the welfare of sentient beings in order to perform the ten kinds of Buddha-activities (v.

22.9). Thereupon, the elder monks—both senior and junior—who had been moved by spiritual urgency upon recollecting the evil deed committed against the Tathāgata at the instigation of the wandering ascetics and mendicants, joined their palms to their heads and [beheld] the Greatly Compassionate Buddha seated upon the great throne.
Having prostrated before the Blessed One, they said this: "10.
The Blessed One has delivered many discourses concerning the Dharma and has prophesied that many beings will attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. 11a.
Following that, in the Anavatapta Lake, in the presence of the Blessed One, we shall each recount our own web of karma. 11b."
It is indeed the natural law (dharmatā) of the Blessed Buddhas—while they are living, remaining, enduring, and maintaining themselves—that there are ten necessary duties to be performed.
What are the ten? The Blessed Buddhas do not enter final nirvana as long as they have not yet made a prophecy concerning a Buddha.
As long as many beings have not yet resolved their minds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
as long as all those to be converted have not been converted;
and as long as the pair of foremost disciples has not been designated.
As long as the boundary has not been established;
as long as the fifth part of his lifespan has not been relinquished;
and as long as the Great Miracle has not been displayed in the great city of Śrāvastī.
Until the descent of the gods has been displayed in the city of Śākāśya;
until my mother and father have been established in the truths; and until my past course of action has been explained to the great lake Anavatapta together with the community of disciples. 13.a.
Then, having taken it to heart, the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, made a prophecy.
Desiring to explain the previous web of karma at Lake Anavatapta, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Having heard those words spoken by the Great Seer..."
Having received the command of the Sugata, those disciples,
the foremost of persons, then departed by means of their supernatural power, just as swans fly through the sky toward the lord of swans.
Just as another [king] would be surrounded by a flock of swans, so too was the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Radiating a manifold web of light-rays, accompanied by nearly five hundred Arhats and surrounded by birds with crimson wings, he, like a great soul, departed from the Jetavana monastery into the air.
He went together with four hundred and ninety-nine who were free from passion.

Then the Blessed One, together with the great community of disciples, vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared at the Great Lake Anavatapta, on the summit of Mount Mahākīṭa to the north of Mount Gandhamādana, situated beyond the Himavat mountains.
That lake in which the heat of the afflictions such as passion does not exist is the great lake Anavatapta; and that [lake]...
Each side is forty-four yojanas;
its depth below is forty yojanas.
It is frequented by fierce yakṣas and is delightful.
It is beautifully adorned with trees bearing various flowers;
from here, four rivers carrying water flow toward the ocean, spreading out in the four directions.
The Ganges, the Indus, the Narmadā, the Vakṣu,
and the Śītā— mortals cannot cross these except by one who has obtained the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*).
Come now, I shall go to the great ocean lake.
It was beautifully adorned with various kinds of diverse flowers and trees bearing sweet-smelling, delicious fruits; furthermore, it was filled with cool, pure, and sweet water,
and graced by blossoms such as the lotus, the blue water-lily, the white water-lily, the fragrant lily, and the red lotus.
Furthermore, it was delightful with the warbling of various birds such as cranes, peacocks, ruddy geese, herons, egrets, ospreys, and curlews;
Then the Buddha, the Blessed One, generates a worldly thought;
at that moment, even down to the smallest ants and insects, they perceive the mind of the Blessed One with their own minds.
Then the two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, reflect: "For what reason has this thought been generated by the Blessed One?"
Knowing through the Buddha’s empowerment that he wished to explain the web of karma at the great lake Anavatapta, those two created for the Blessed One,

in the middle of the great lake Anavatapta, a golden lotus as his seat— measuring a cartwheel in size, with a thousand petals, a shimmering jeweled stalk, beautiful filaments, and composed of the five precious gems. Therein, they manifested it.

The Blessed One sat down, and the monks also sat down facing the Blessed One upon other lotus calyxes. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain sewing his outer robe (saṃghāṭī).
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Go, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and bring a companion for the going-forth.

"So be it, Blessed One," the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the Blessed One's words. Having vanished from the great lake Anavatapta, he appeared on Vulture Peak Mountain in the presence of the Venerable Śāriputra and spoke thus.

"Śāriputra, the Teacher, together with four hundred and ninety-nine arhats, is staying at the great lake Anavatapta, desiring to explain the past web of karma; he remains waiting for you, so come, let us go.
Śāriputra said:
“Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I shall first sew my outer robe and then come.
Then Maudgalyāyana, unable to endure those words, bound five fingers upon him by means of his supernatural power;
he too, remaining in the act of sewing, stood firm through his own great supernatural power.
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if that is so, let it be a robe made of patches.
Maudgalyāyana said, "Venerable Śāriputra, if you will not go, then this robe must be sewn by me."
"After that, you shall go.
Venerable Śāriputra, I shall provide assistance.
Śāriputra said:
"Do so.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana began to sew with his five fingers by means of his supernatural power.
He was addressed by the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if that is so, let it be another sūtra.
He replied,
"Venerable Śāriputra, if you do not go after having done this..."
"I shall lead you there by the power of my supernatural faculties.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra, having loosened the blindfold over his eyes, said:
"For you, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, have been declared by the Blessed One to be the foremost among those possessed of supernatural faculties."
"First, you will surely carry me away by force.
Then he was pulled back by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra reflected:
"Endowed with great supernatural power and great majesty,
it is possible that he will summon [the mountain].
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra summoned Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
He was pulled along by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. As they reached Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain,
the Venerable Śāriputra thought, "He will pull even Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain along with him."
The Venerable Śāriputra tied it to Sumeru, the king of mountains,
and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana pulled it;
at that time, even Sumeru, the king of mountains, was shaken.
Then the two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, were also agitated.
When they become agitated, the monks question the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, why are the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda agitated?"
"By whom was the great lake Anavatapta agitated?
The Blessed One said,
"Monks, it was not the two dragon kings Nanda and Upananda who agitated it."
Moreover, as the two great śrāvakas performed a great display of supernatural powers against one another,
the Venerable Śāriputra reflected:
"This man will even drag away Sumeru, the king of mountains."
Therefore, the lotus stalk was fastened to that very lotus pericarp upon which the Blessed One was seated;
thus, it remained perfectly still.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"You have performed a great display of miraculous power;
let it be so, come, let us go.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I too shall come alone until the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana departs.
Then the venerable Śāriputra, having arrived first, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down upon the pericarp of his own lotus-seat.
Thereafter, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arrived and took his place upon his own seat.
He was addressed by him:
"Venerable Śāriputra, have you come?
He replied:
"I have come. Then all the monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One:

"Behold, Bhadanta, how the Blessed One has designated the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana as the foremost among those possessed of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), being one of great psychic might and great majesty."
He too was defeated by the venerable Śāriputra through supernatural power.
The Blessed One said: "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, he was defeated by this very craft. 25
Listen to this, monks. Once upon a time, there was a master painter in the Middle Country.
On some business, he went to the realm of the Yavanas and stayed at the house of a master artisan of mechanical devices; having settled there, he took his meals and so forth.
Therefore, he had a wooden mechanical doll made and sent as an attendant;
that wooden mechanical doll stood there holding an oil massage in her hand.
Then she was addressed by him:
"Come here!
She remained silent.
He reflected, "Surely a female attendant must have been sent to serve me."
She was described thus:
"Aha! By the Creator, a woman has been fashioned as if born from jewels;
by her, my eyes have been purified through my merit."

"Fie! Alas for the birth of that man in Jambudvīpa, who does not possess such a young woman—endowed with beauty and youth, supremely enchanting—who might be honored by him through the eye, the hand, or the touch of her body! Having been thus honored with these words of sweetness resembling nectar, he began to collect [the goods].
"Dear Sundarī, come, come here!
Even so, perceiving that the wooden mechanical doll had not said anything at all, his mind overcome by passion, he quickly approached;
having seized her with his hand and pulled her, she then stood there as a mere heap of wooden joints.
He was mocked with derision.
He reflected:
"I have been singled out for mockery by him."

Thinking, "I too shall act in such a way that he will fall into public ridicule and derision in the midst of the assembly together with the king," he painted a figure of himself with a noose around its neck facing the door;
immediately thereafter, he remained hidden, crouching behind the surface of the door-panel.
At the time of his rising,
that master mechanic, having observed that the sun had already passed its zenith, reflected:
"The day has become too late."
"For whose sake does he not let this [child] go out?
Having gone there,
he saw him.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"For what reason has he hanged himself?
Then, as he looked, he saw a heap of wooden beams and recognized them.
He was killed by Pratibhinna.
And this is the custom here in the realm of the Yavanas:
whenever a guest dies in someone's house, he passes away to the other world.
He remained in that state until it was reported to the king.
He reported to the king:
"Your Majesty, a master painter has arrived here from the Middle Country; he has descended into my residence, and I have sent him a female wooden mechanical puppet as an attendant."
Having been seized by him with that hand and pulled out, she then remained as a heap of wooden joints. He then hanged himself with that very cord.
"Your Majesty, please examine this first; afterwards, I shall perform the funeral rites."
By the king's command, the ministers went there;
they saw him,
and having seen him, they said:
"How should he be brought down from our elephant-tusk?
Others said,
"The snare must be cut."
Taking up an axe, he began to cut the snare;
as soon as it was severed, that master mechanic stood there with his eyes wide open in astonishment.
Emerging from behind the door-panel, he said:
"O man, I was confounded by you alone;
but you, in turn, were confounded by me in the midst of the assembly including the king.
What do you think, monks?
That master painter was none other than this monk Śāriputra;
that master mechanic was none other than this monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Even then, he was defeated by him through that very craft.
Even now he has been defeated by him. Listen further to how he was defeated by him in the past.
Once upon a time, monks...
A dispute arose between two master painters;
one said,
"I know a beautiful craft."
The other said, "I know a beautiful craft. Then, out of their dispute, they approached the king together; having approached him, they spoke in the presence of the king, "I know a beautiful craft."
The other also said, "I too know a beautiful craft.
Then the king pointed out the gateway chamber and said,
"Gentlemen, I do not know which of you knows the craft."
"However, let one of you polish one wall, and the second polish the other; thus, having placed a curtain between them, the two began to paint.
One of them completed the work of painting in six months.
The second also completed the work on the walls within six months;
he who had performed the painting work approached the king,
and having approached him, he said:
"Your Majesty, my work of painting is finished;
let the Great King behold it.
The king, accompanied by his ministers, went out.
The king saw it;
having seen it, he said, "This work of painting is excellent.
The second one also said, "Your Majesty, please behold this work of painting."
The shadow fell upon it;
seeing this, the king remarked, "This painting-work is exceedingly clear.
He too drew back the curtain and said:
"This is not a work of painting, but rather the preparation of a wall.
Thus the king was filled with wonder.
He addressed his ministers, saying, "Sirs, this artisan is most excellent.
What do you think, monks?
He who performed the work on the wall in six months was this very same monk Śāriputra;
he who performed the work of painting in six months was [the other].

"This very person is that monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana; even then he was defeated by means of his craft, and now too he has been defeated by means of his supernatural power (ṛddhi). Furthermore, he was again defeated by means of supernatural power.
Listen to that:
in ancient times, there were two sages named Śaṅkha and Likhita in Vārāṇasī;
between them there arose a dispute due to a disagreement over whether it was raining or not.
Then once, when Śaṅkha did not ask him with his feet, the matted-haired Jaṭa, provoked to anger, said to him: "May your head split open like the rising sun!"
Śaṅkha said, "The sun will not rise at my word.
When he had spoken thus, the world remained in total darkness for a very long time.
Out of compassion, he fashioned for him a head made of clay;
then, at sunrise, it suddenly shattered into a hundred pieces upon the earth.
In another birth, that Śaṅkha has today become Maudgalyāyana;
this Likhita is Śāriputra, who was his victor even then.

Even now, he was defeated by him through supernatural power; this and more should be understood in detail. (28.b) Those meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) which the Tathāgata has attained, even the names of those the Pratyekabuddhas do not know.
Those which the Pratyekabuddhas have attained, even Śāriputra does not know even the names of those.
Śāriputra does not even know the names of those [attainments] which Maudgalyāyana possesses;
and other disciples do not even know the names of those which Maudgalyāyana possesses.

Therefore, this Śāriputra is of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*). However, he was designated by me as the foremost among those with supernatural powers with reference to those who dwell in manifold states. 29
Immediately after this, he said:
"Having gone there, he should utter words that are in accordance with his former dwellings and past conduct."
He who remembers there what was done here— both auspicious and inauspicious karma— shall experience the arising of happiness.
Then the elder monks, by the command of the Tathāgata, each recounted his own web of karma.
First of all, Mahāpratibhāna Nāgila said:
"The monk named Nāgila was a disciple of the Buddha."
Being asked a question, he gave an explanation at the great lake Anavatapta.
Then a monk named Nāgila, having joined his ten fingers in reverent salutation before the Tathāgata, declared his own web of karma:
"Having given the *kaṭhina* robe to the Saṃgha with a mind of great faith,
I have not known a miserable rebirth for thirty great eons from this point back."
For eighteen eons I have delighted in the world of the gods;
sixty-four times indeed have I exercised the sovereignty of the lord of gods.
And eight thousand times have I been a universal monarch.
The number of local kings, however, is not known to me.
Aha! Wherever humans perform service for the Triple Gem, even by giving only a small amount, they obtain a vast fruit. (3–4)

If, having abandoned great divine happiness, my birth is among mortals, and I am honored by mortals, that is the fruit of the gift of the mat. If there should be rebirth as a god, having abandoned human happiness...
I am worthy of worship by the assembly of gods; that is the fruit of my gift of the *kaṭhina*.
Taking the entire circle of the earth and oceans as far as the Cakravāḍa mountains, I shall today, if I so desire, cover it all with fine cloth.
Again, speaking of the excellence of the gift of the *kaṭhina*, he said:
"With every step I take, fine cotton cloths appear before me;
I stand upon these cloths, and there is even a canopy of fine cloth. (8)
The states of existence have been opened up for me, and the afflictions have been overcome by me;
all outflows are completely exhausted—this is the fruit of that firm gift.
The four analytical knowledges, the [eight] liberations, and likewise the eight [bases of mastery]— [are attained].
Having attained the six supernormal knowledges, the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.
Possessing a fragrant body, going to the world of the gods, with great wealth and natural enjoyments, he is a master of happiness.

Indeed, through the offering of fragrance, one who is traveling toward liberation will have the scent of pure virtue wafting through the directions. Those endowed with faith who offer flowers to the Sugata in the assembly of the Saṅgha— 30.2 30.2.1 [Flower]— will [attain this].
Like flowers, those liberated ones who follow the heavenly path of all worlds shine forth;
endowed with the fragrance of true virtue, they are incessantly honored by gods and asuras alike.
From their bodies, a supreme scent emanates, and the sense of smell of these happy beings becomes purified.
One should cause a diverse and thick garland to be offered to the assembly of deities;
one’s headache will not be felt, and one becomes a sky-walker. Those who offer incense with sincere devotion to the assembly of the Enemy of Manmatha—verse 30.3.

Those who possess moral discipline attain constant happiness; being joyful, they become lords of enjoyments. Their mindfulness does not falter; having gained a firm footing in the meditative absorptions, they become self-controlled. Possessing captivating minds and sharp intellects, these venerable ones attain peace, honored by gods and asuras alike. (Dhūpa 30.4)
He possesses eyes that are a delight to behold, with large blue eyes; his treasury is well-filled,
and he is one to be gazed upon by both men and women.
He who offers a garland of lamps to the Saṅgha— such a person possesses a radiant complexion, soft hands and feet,
great strength, and cannot be overcome by enemies.
By the gift of oil, mortals become possessed of beautiful forms and attain happiness. [30.6] One who gives shoes with a joyful mind— [30.6.1]
He shall be a possessor of supernatural powers and rich in wealth;
that great-souled one will have well-proportioned feet, will frequent the heavens, and will travel in excellent vehicles.
As soon as that Sage was born, taking his first seven steps upon the earth with great strength,
a row of lotuses was formed, which indeed became the fruit [of his action].
How could that gift of a pair of sandals exist otherwise?
By the gift of an umbrella, one becomes a protector from the heat for the worlds;
through the delightful shade [it provides], one dwells for a very long time with the royal splendor of playful ease.
He will certainly become a lord of Dharma and a protector of the entire world;
endowed with beauty and obtaining enjoyments, he shall not go to the thicket of evil destinies.
Having first placed [the child] upon his lap, the Great-Souled One was filled with joy.
In former times, while the relics of Kāśyapa were within the parasol,
the high-souled Nanda experienced happiness both in heaven and on earth, and then attained peace. (Chattrasūtra 30.8)
By the gift of a needle for a thread, one certainly attains wisdom;
through the attainment of wisdom, that treasury of intelligence is liberated from the fears of the states of existence.
Wisdom is the queen in the removal of misfortune; there is no other like it.
She becomes fully accomplished, possessing fruit in every respect.
(Sūtrasūcī 30.9) He who gives chalk here—pure like crystal and measuring twelve finger-breadths—will be born as a great scholar. (Khaṭikā 30.10; 30.10.1)
Endowed with wealth, possessing a face that captivates the eyes with its fragrance, having a charming voice free from diseases such as excessive phlegm,
and being devoid of mental afflictions, he partakes in the birth among the gods;
such is the activity of one whose sprout has germinated through the gift of betel.
His face is marked with auspicious signs, his eyes are beautiful,
his lips are copper-colored, his rows of teeth are lustrous and delicate,
and his lovely cheeks are free from phlegmatic diseases and parasites.
This is the foremost fruit resulting from the gift of betel-leaf. [30.11] Betel-leaf [30.11.1]:
[The merit of giving] necklaces made of lapis lazuli and gold, adorned with pearls, which rest upon the neck, head, feet, and arms;
Whether in heaven or on earth, they declare that clothing is the most excellent ornament for the decoration of the body;
for even one endowed with beauty, born of noble lineage, and possessed of discernment—
Even one who has exerted effort in many scriptural traditions and is fully adorned with a multitude of virtues such as ethical discipline does not truly shine on this earth without clothing.
Therefore, having observed that clothing is an incomparable ornament and a protection against cold, heat, gadflies, and mosquitoes,
those who have attained their desires should repeatedly bestow the gift of garments upon men— the peerless garment of modesty.
Seated upon a lion throne with golden fly-whisks shimmering like moonbeams and white parasols held aloft,
he was adorned on his head with crowns of gold and jewels.
Even a glorious universal monarch does not shine without clothing.
[Likewise,] even in the city of Alakā where the illustrious Lord of Wealth dwells, or in Bhogavatī adorned with the jewels of a thousand tongues,
or upon the peaks of Kailāsa and Meru in the midst of the hosts of gods—
Even Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra do not shine without clothing.

He possesses divine, exquisite garments; among the hosts of the sons of the Sugata, he is handsome and charming; his self is adorned with the garment of modesty; he is sharp-witted and a sovereign over all dharmas. (30.12) With necklaces, half-necklaces, and many bracelets...
Adorned with various armlets and bracelets, mortals move about after having offered diverse ornaments to a disciple of the Sugata. (Ābharaṇa 30.13)
Neither fire nor poison enters his body, nor does a weapon, nor even a rain of thunderbolts;
this is due to the gift of copper and other metals to the Saṅgha of the Jina.
A mortal who dwells in loving-kindness performs [this].
In whatever place a person is reborn, they become worthy of worship and salutation with vessels of copper and other metals;
having attained heaven, they possess abundant wealth and are highly esteemed in the assemblies of the virtuous.

One is born into a high, illustrious, and very great family, becoming one who enjoys pleasures, attains peace, and possesses incomparable qualities as a donor of a seat. By the gift of a seat (30.15), one becomes powerful, endowed with a secure position, a king of great prosperity.
Having given food to the Saṅgha, one prospers in happiness everywhere. Born into a high family, he becomes virtuous,
worthy of being served by men, and beautiful to behold.
Through the offering of *śāli* rice and sacrificial cakes, he becomes gracious, wise, happy, golden-hued, and glorious;
by offering *camasa*, *laḍḍuka*, *pūraka*, and *paulika* sweets. (30.17)
By offering various cakes, *karambha*, and *parpaṭa*,
as well as *satakraka* (sour gruel) to the excellent Gaṇa, one becomes a lord devoted to enjoyments. (30.18) [Laddukas, etc.]
Those men who, having placed curd, soma, clarified butter, honey, sugar, and molasses into vessels made of gold, silver, and other materials, offer them to the Gaṇas;

The five kinds of nectar-eaters, endowed with strength, having filled a jar with water and offered it to the supreme Gaṇa, enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure and sever eternal craving. (Pañcasāra 30.19; Kumbha 30.20)
By the gift of a water-pot and an alms-bowl, one becomes endowed with the knowledge of the Dharma and is born equal to the Giver of Wealth (Vaiśravaṇa) within the Triple Gem.
By giving a house to the best of the Gaṇas, one becomes a "giver of all" (sarvadada) and,
with all desires fulfilled, prospers in happiness everywhere. (30.21–22)
By that very gift of the wish-fulfilling tree, he shall become complete;
as a human being in Uttarakuru, he will possess great enjoyments.
The great merit of the gift of a bell is that one becomes handsome and always joyful in mind.
One who, with a pure intention, bestows various medicinal provisions upon the Saṅgha, becomes like a king of the Gandharvas, possessing speech that is pleasing to both gods and asuras. (Ghaṇṭā 30.24)
He is not touched by the sufferings arising from the intermediate kalpa of disease; liberated from sickness, old age, and the like, he lives happily with undivided resolve,
for one who is free from the disease of the afflictions attains ultimate health.
In the past, he went for medicine and was provided with bark garments;
there, in that healthy community, he requested medicine.

Out of compassion for his welfare, one who was free from passion ate a single *harītakī* fruit, and by that act, he brought it to completion. For five hundred births, not even the slightest illness occurred to him.
With body, speech, and mind purified, free from torment like one who has cast off a sword, he is happy;
he destroys craving and does not merely abandon it—he abandons even the craving for cyclic existence.
(30.25.2) This was [spoken] by the monk Yaśomitra in the teaching of Kāśyapa.
For twelve thousand years, water was distributed to the community.

By the ripening of that karma, for five hundred births he did not experience the suffering caused by thirst even in his dreams. (2) Those who joyfully offer to the Saṅgha a refreshing drink that cuts off craving— (30.26) [they shall attain such a state].

Having cut with wisdom the creeper of craving— which arises from the passion for existence, which is heart-pleasing, endowed with sweet flavors, sharp in taste, delightful in fragrance, and dear— those who give this auspicious drink certainly reach the further shore of the ocean of existence. (Pānaka 30.27)
Having reached the land bounded by the ocean, that king of men attained the palaces of monarchs who possessed immeasurable wealth, were endowed with horses and elephants, and had vast retinues.
One who, endowed with faith, bestows upon the Saṅgha land yielding various grains and fruits, is born with supreme luster and beauty. (Bhūmi 30.28)
Its desired fruit ripens constantly;
every fruit matures upon the path to awakening. Merit is like a lamp in the darkness for human beings.
He is protection in times of fear, a kinsman in times of calamity, the unsurpassed medicine for diseases, and a boat in the great ocean of saṃsāra. (31.2)
Wealth comes through giving, not from harming others; heaven through ethical conduct, not from leaping off mountain precipices;
purity through truthfulness, not from entering water.
Liberation comes through knowledge, not from the emaciation of the body. By not giving what has been given, one becomes poor;
and because of poverty, one commits evil deeds.
Having committed evil, one goes to hell;
even when released from hell, one remains an evildoer. Generosity destroys poverty; ethical conduct destroys rebirth in the lower realms.
Wisdom is the destroyer of ignorance; meditative cultivation is the destroyer of worldly existence.
When a person gives their own wealth with a pure mind, at that very moment, the two aggregates of merit are designated as "giving."
May Lakṣmī, blazing brilliantly, dwell here forever; may Fame, ever-shining, [dwell here];
may the Lord of the Earth, having utterly destroyed his enemies, protect the earth for a long time, free from disease and famine;
and may those worthy of offerings, rich in virtue, constantly attain growth in the collection of the teachings.
May the unshakable teaching of the Blessed One triumph, shining as long as the moon and sun exist!
May the lord of the earth rule the world according to the Dharma,
and may people become devoted to the worship of the Three Jewels.
May families with vast herds of cattle, their sins stilled, always rejoice; and may subjects with noble offspring ever prosper.
As long as the sun of hot radiance shines in the sky, so long do the young camels appear beautiful.
The moon, its orb matted with rays, has been set in motion;
as long as the lotus-dwelling deities flash forth upon their own earth, may the teaching of the Sugata, honored by gods and asuras, remain unimpeded. 32B.
Then the elder monks questioned the Blessed One:
"What karma was performed by the Blessed One?"
"By the ripening of which karma was the Blessed One’s big toe wounded by a stone fragment when he had attained perfect enlightenment?
The Blessed One said,
"Monks, these actions were performed by the Tathāgata himself," and so on in detail.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons; having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
Long ago, monks, in a past age incalculable eons back, there lived a householder in a certain mountain district.
He took a wife who was his equal.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her.
While he was playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, a son was born.
He was raised and grew up until he became a great man.
Then, at a later time, the wife of that householder passed away.
He took another wife, and while he was sporting, enjoying himself, and taking pleasure with her, a son was born to him.
He then provided a residence for his eldest son;
while that son was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a son was born to him and a daughter was also born.
Then, at a later time, the householder passed away along with his wife.
That boy remained in the presence of his own brother. Then that householder’s son was addressed by his wife:
"Noble son, this boy belongs to you."
"This man is my brother.
She said,
"Noble son, a share of the house must also be given to him."
He said,
"Half belongs to you, and half belongs to us.
She said:
"Noble son, having become the name of this one man, half shall belong to us who are many, and half shall belong to him.
He said,
"This is the way of the world."
She said, "Noble son, if it is so, then have him killed. He replied,
"My dear lady, how indeed could I kill my own brother for the sake of wealth?"
She said to him again and again,
"For one who indulges in sensual pleasures, there is indeed no evil deed that should not be committed.
He consented to this.
He said to his brother:
"Brother, let us go to the forest for the sake of gathering flowers."
He went with him;
there, having thrown him into a mountain cave, he struck him down with a stone. What do you think, monks?
He who was that householder’s son,
by whom that half-brother was caused to be killed for the sake of his inheritance,
was none other than I at that time and on that occasion.
Because I killed my half-brother for the sake of his wealth,
as the ripening of that karma, I was reborn in the hells for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years.
By the remainder of that very karma, even now, while the Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment, my foot has been wounded by a stone fragment.
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Blessed One, the ripening of which resulted in his foot being wounded by a thorn of acacia wood when he had attained full enlightenment?
It was by the Tathāgata himself, monks, that these karmas were performed," and so on in detail.
"In the past, monks, there were two caravan leaders who, having skillfully prepared a sea-going vessel, set out upon the great ocean to fetch wealth."
By a favorable wind, they reached the Island of Jewels; there,
one of them filled his vessel with jewels, while the second filled his with food.
The two set out; there,
the boat belonging to the one who had filled it beyond its capacity met with disaster.
Having weighed [the goods] with that caravan leader using a scale and removed the jewels, the caravan leader addressed him;
he reflected:
"This man will go away having achieved his purpose, while I shall go away having failed in my purpose."
He began to pierce that vehicle;
while he was piercing it, he was seen by the caravan leader,
who said, "Do not pierce the vehicle."
"Lest we all fall into calamity through such misconduct," he said;
yet, even though being restrained, he did not stop. He was killed by that blow of the spear.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that caravan leader, by whom [I] was struck down with a blow of a spear—
at that time, on that occasion, he was none other than myself, who was struck down by that blow of a spear.
As the ripening of that karma, he was reborn in the hells for many hundreds of years, many millions of billions of years.
By the remainder of that very same karma, the foot of the Tathāgata, once he had attained perfect enlightenment, was wounded by a thorn of *khadira* wood.
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Blessed One, the ripening of which resulted in his being falsely accused by the young woman Sundarikā?"
"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself," and so on in detail,
"until they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings. Long ago, monks, in the past, [this occurred].
When the lifespan of humanity was eighty thousand years, a teacher named Vipaśyin arose in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Bhagavat.
By the teaching of the Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin, two brothers, Vasiṣṭha and Bharadvāja, went forth as monastics.
Through the abandonment of all defilements, Vasiṣṭha realized arhatship.
While Bharadvāja was reciting and studying his lessons, he mastered the three Piṭakas; he became a master of the Tripiṭaka, possessing ready and eloquent inspired speech.
The householder was thus won over by him;
for his sake, he had a monastery constructed, fully equipped with all necessary requisites.
Then it occurred to that [other] brother: "Come, let us dwell together in one place."
Having gone there, he was seen by that householder.
Upon seeing the Arhat monk, who was serene in body and serene in mind, he became full of faith.
Out of the faith thus born, he honored him and clothed him in a most precious garment.
He was seen by that brother,
who thought, "I am this householder's foremost companion in all matters;
he covers himself with a cloth, thinking 'he is covered,' and has thus become one who watches for a lapse in his presence."
He was seen by him while he was thus preoccupied; he reflected, "If I give this to him,
he will enter into an even greater state of faith," and so he bestowed it upon him,
saying, "Let it be yours alone."
A maidservant of that householder came to that monastery and performed the maintenance work; she was addressed by him:
"Maid, I give this pair of garments to you."
"You must do as I say.
She said,
"Noble sir, what must I do?"
"You, having put on that pair of garments, perform the household chores.

If the householder asks, 'From where did you get this pair of garments?', you should say, 'It was given to me by such-and-such a noble one. If he asks, 'For whose sake was it given to you by the noble one?'"
The noble one should say this, and he should also ask: "For what purpose do men bestow [garments] upon women?
She, having put on that garment, began to perform the household chores.
That garment was recognized by the householder.
She was addressed by him:
"Maiden, from where did you get this pair of garments?
She replied:
"This was given to me by this noble one.
"Daughter, for what reason has this pair of garments been bestowed upon you by the noble one?
She replied:
"Noble one, this too should be asked:
for what reason do men bestow [gifts] upon women?
He then began to manifest his lack of faith toward him.
Those great beings are fearful of being treated with disrespect;
having risen, he departed.
What do you think, monks?
He who was named Bharadvāja, by whom that Arhat was falsely accused— that was myself at that time, on that occasion; because I falsely accused that Arhat monk,
as the ripening of that karma, I was reborn in the hells for many hundreds of thousands of years and many hundreds of millions of years.
"By the remainder of that very same karma, the Tathāgata is now falsely accused by the young woman Sundarikā," and so forth, in detail.
